title: Monumentum Adulitanum II — an Aksumite king's throne inscription at Adulis, §62 (the Red Sea crossing)
language_note: Koine Greek, cut on a stone throne at Adulis by an Aksumite king writing in the language of the Roman east about his own conquests. The same language as africa-03-periplus-adulis and arabia-01, and the point of the record is that here it is an AFRICAN king using it, not a Greek merchant describing him.
date: 3rd century CE on the usual dating of the king; the text as transmitted dates from Cosmas Indicopleustes' copy of the early 520s, which is the date of the copy and not of the monument. The corpus records both rather than choosing: the monument's own date is disputed and nothing here settles it.
findspot: Adulis (Zula), on the Eritrean Red Sea coast. The throne and its inscription no longer survive; the text exists only because Cosmas Indicopleustes copied it there c. 520 CE and included it in his Christian Topography (2.60-63).
original_text_excerpt: ταῦτα δὲ πάντα τὰ ἔθνη ὄρεσιν ἰσχυροῖς πεφρουρημένα αὐτὸς ἐγὼ ἐν ταῖς μάχαις παρὼν νικήσας καὶ ὑποτάξας ἐχαρισάμην αὐτοῖς πάσας τὰς χώρας ἐπὶ φόροις. ἄλλα δὲ πλεῖστα ἔθνη ἑκόντα ὑπετάγη μοι ἐπὶ φόροις. καὶ πέραν δὲ τῆς Ἐρυθρᾶς θαλάσσης οἰκοῦντας Ἀρραβίτας καὶ Κιναιδοκολπίτας στράτευμα ναυτικὸν καὶ πεζικὸν διαπεμψάμενος καὶ ὑποτάξας αὐτῶν τοὺς βασιλέας φόρους τῆς γῆς τελεῖν ἐκέλευσα καὶ ὁδεύεσθαι μετ’ εἰρήνης καὶ πλέεσθαι, ἀπό τε Λευκῆς κώμης ἕως τῶν Σαβαίων χώρας ἐπολέμησα.
original_text_note:
Verbatim Koine Greek, §62 of the throne inscription as Cosmas Indicopleustes transmits it, in the text W. Dittenberger prints in OGIS I (1903), no. 199, pp. 292-294, collated on 2026-09-23 against the University of Toronto scan (https://archive.org/details/orientisgraeciin01dittuoft). RULING 98: the edition's characters stand. The text was first copied by hand from PHI Greek Inscriptions on 2026-08-31, where it follows Wolska-Conus's later edition; the collation found three differences, now applied -- two commas OGIS does not print, and OGIS's spelling of the first people named, with a double rho. Editorial acts, declared: OGIS's line numbers, note numbers, division strokes, margin letters, and the reference marks to the scholia printed in its right-hand column are omitted, and line-break hyphens are closed up. The apostrophe in μετ’ εἰρήνης is U+2019. Nothing else is altered.

PHI IS A CROSS-REFERENCE, NOT THE SOURCE. epigraphy.packhum.org/text/219054 restricts use to personal study (RULING 98), and nothing here is quoted from it.
reference_translation: All these nations, protected though they were by mountains all but impregnable, I conquered, after engagements in which I was myself present. Upon their submission I restored their territories to them, subject to the payment of tribute. Many other tribes besides these submitted of their own accord, and became likewise tributary. And I sent a fleet and land forces against the Arabitae and Cinaedocolpitae who dwelt on the other side of the Red Sea, and having reduced the sovereigns of both, I imposed on them a land tribute and charged them to make travelling safe both by sea and by land. I thus subdued the whole coast from Leucê Cômê to the country of the Sabaeans.
translation_source: J. W. McCrindle, The Christian Topography of Cosmas, an Egyptian Monk (Hakluyt Society, 1897), Book II, translating the same section; public domain, transcribed at the Tertullian Project, https://www.tertullian.org/fathers/cosmas_02_book2.htm. Copied by hand from that page on 2026-08-31. McCrindle's footnote reference markers and the Hakluyt edition's marginal page numbers are removed; his wording and spellings — including 'Leucê Cômê' and 'Cinaedocolpitae' — are unaltered.
citation_original: W. Dittenberger, Orientis Graeci Inscriptiones Selectae I (Leipzig: Hirzel, 1903), no. 199 (from p. 285), the §62 passage at pp. 292-294 = Kosmas Indikopleustes, Topographia Christiana 2.60-63. Public domain. Scan: Internet Archive, orientisgraeciin01dittuoft (University of Toronto copy).
notes: F4, record 31, and Sub-Saharan Africa's second record carrying retrieval-eligible source-language text. WHY THIS SECTION: §62 is the passage that touches Rome rather than Aksum's own hinterland. The king sends a fleet and an army across the Red Sea, subdues the kings of the Arabitae and Kinaidokolpitai, and orders the routes kept safe by land and sea from Λευκῆς κώμης to the country of the Sabaeans — and Leuke Kome is the Roman Red Sea port the Periplus names, which this corpus already holds in two records. The link is a named place shared with arabia-01 and africa-03, not a thematic resemblance. READ THIS RECORD BESIDE RULING 58: it is Greek, and it is the second Greek record filling Africa's per-region source-language floor. That the floor can be met in the language of the empire is a gap no check here can see, and the ruling says so rather than leaving it to be noticed at G3. The record is a good one and the floor being met this way is a separate question; the two must not blur. NOT gloss-capable: the text carries no alternative or hedged reading, and F4's two gloss-capable records are owed elsewhere.
